native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: Higher time preference (proxied by 1989 savings behaviour: taking money out of savings or having no savings, vs putting money in) is significantly associated with higher BMI in the NLSY79 cohort — respondents taking money out had BMI +0.51 (1989) and +0.62 (1992) higher; those with no savings +0.79 (1989) and +0.93 (1992) higher — after adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, family income, family size, parental education and ASVAB; the association persists after controlling baseline BMI and corresponds to ~28–31% higher obesity odds. Wealth-accumulation proxy is directionally consistent but not significant. Observational association; not causal.
native_result.WorkflowB: Derived BMI (703*lb/in^2) at 1981/1989/1992 using decoded 1981 and 1985 heights; defined time-preference proxy A = 1989 savings direction (ref: put money in) and proxy B = bottom-quarter net wealth & wealth-income ratio; ran OLS (HC1 robust SE) of BMI1989 (primary, same-survey-year) and BMI1992 (forward check) on savings dummies plus 11 confounders; robustness: controlling BMI1981, obesity logistic (OR), proxy B, unadjusted reference, and complete-vs-incomplete group comparison; diagnostics VIF and residual checks.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.

sub_hypo.text: In the NLSY79 cohort, higher time preference, proxied by taking money out of savings or having no savings in 1989 rather than putting money in, is significantly associated with higher BMI in 1989 and 1992 after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, parental-education and ASVAB covariates. The association persists after controlling for baseline BMI and corresponds to approximately 28–31% higher obesity odds. A wealth-accumulation proxy is directionally consistent but not statistically significant. These are observational, not causal, associations.
sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 respondents; savings behaviour measured in 1989, with BMI1989 as the primary same-survey-year outcome, BMI1992 as a forward check, and BMI1981 as the baseline robustness control.
variables: Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989
Derived BMI in 1981, 1989 and 1992 (703 × weight in pounds / height in inches squared)
Total net family income (measurement year not specified)
Highest grade completed by respondent's mother, 1979
Highest grade completed by respondent's father, 1979
Family net wealth (measurement year not specified)
Derived time-preference proxy B: bottom-quarter net wealth and wealth-income ratio
sub_hypo.relations: Adjusted OLS with HC1 robust standard errors associates taking money out of savings, relative to putting money in, with BMI higher by 0.51 in 1989 and 0.62 in 1992; having no savings is associated with BMI higher by 0.79 and 0.93, respectively. These positive associations are significant after covariate adjustment and persist when controlling BMI1981. Obesity logistic models indicate approximately 28–31% higher odds with higher time preference. The wealth-accumulation proxy has a directionally consistent but nonsignificant association. No causal relationship is asserted.
